<reason>Both sides argued well and the debate narrowed cleanly to one fork: does the next dollar buy more by thickening ties inside already-open rooms (PRO) or by finding the person who never enters them (CON). PRO's structural point—that every CON success ends in a place or a known person, and that much urban loneliness belongs to mobile people served directly by late hours—was sound and partly unanswered by CON's "they have phones" reply. But CON did more damage with less: it extracted and then exploited PRO's own concessions ("welcoming one more costs near zero," hours "don't teleport the never-visitor"), turned PRO's Chicago example into a case of lit branches that still left the isolated to die, correctly flagged PRO's "rooms go dark" framing as not the motion, and used PRO's librarian-outreach answer to argue "fund the list." CON's closing seizure of PRO's own final line ("nothing takes care of itself") was the sharpest moment. CON's reframing of "apps" as volunteer-coordination software is somewhat convenient and its marginal-cost logic has a slip PRO never fully exposed, and CON's first rebuttal was clipped—these keep the margin modest. Overall CON made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 exploiting B's own pressure answer: hours "don't teleport the never-visitor" and only convert existing visitors into regulars, so "sensors only sense members" and the homebound woman is invisible to every PRO mechanism—compounded in closing by turning "the doorbell takes care of itself" into the assumption that killed Chicago's isolated seniors.</best_rebuttal>
